entry: Indian politician and former film actor, chief minister of [[Tamil Nadu]] since May 10, 2026. Before entering politics he was a leading actor in Tamil cinema and among the highest-paid actors in India, with commercial successes such as *Thuppakki* (2012), *Mersal* (2017) and *Leo* (2023). In February 2024 he announced his retirement from films and launched the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) party. The TVK emerged as the single-largest party in the 2026 Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly election, winning 108 seats, and Vijay was sworn in with the support of several smaller allied parties.

British writer, literary scholar and [[Anglicanism|Anglican]] lay theologian. He held academic posts in English literature at Magdalen College, [[University of Oxford|Oxford]] (1925–1954), and Magdalene College, Cambridge (1954–1963). He is best known for *The Chronicles of Narnia*, a seven-book fantasy series for children, and also wrote *The Screwtape Letters* and the *Space Trilogy*, as well as works of [[Apologetics|Christian apologetics]] such as *Mere Christianity* and *Miracles*. A close friend of [[J. R. R. Tolkien]], he belonged to the Inklings, an informal Oxford literary group. Baptized in the Church of Ireland, he became an [[Atheism|atheist]] in adolescence and returned to Anglicanism at age 32. His wartime radio broadcasts on Christianity brought him wide acclaim. His more than 30 books have sold millions of copies. In 2013 a memorial to him was placed in Poets' Corner in [[Westminster Abbey]].

General-purpose, multi-paradigm programming language from [[Microsoft]]. Its principal designers were Anders Hejlsberg, Scott Wiltamuth and Peter Golde, and it was first widely distributed in July 2000. Ecma International approved it as ECMA-334 in 2002, and ISO/IEC followed in 2003. Introduced with the .NET Framework and Visual Studio, both initially closed-source, it gained an open-source, cross-platform ecosystem: the Mono project began in 2004, and a decade later Microsoft released Visual Studio Code, Roslyn and the unified .NET platform. The latest stable version, C# 15.0, was released in 2026 with .NET 11.0.

Indian physicist known for research on light [[Scattering|scattering]]. With his student K. S. Krishnan, he discovered in 1928 that light traversing a transparent material changes its [[Wavelength|wavelength]] when deflected, a phenomenon now called the Raman effect. Raman received the [[Nobel Prize]] in Physics in 1930, becoming the first Asian and non-White person to win a Nobel Prize in Physics. His major contributions were in [[Acoustics|acoustics]] and [[Optics|optics]]. He became the first Indian director of the Indian Institute of Science in [[Bengaluru]] in 1933 and founded the Raman Research Institute in 1948. The Government of India celebrates the day of the discovery, February 28, as National Science Day.

High-level, general-purpose programming language created by Danish computer scientist Bjarne Stroustrup, first released in 1985 as an extension of [[C (programming language)|C]]. It added object-oriented features, later functional programming features, and generic programming through templates. C++ has been used to create and maintain [[Microsoft Windows]] and is widely applied in systems software, video games and servers. The latest ISO standard, ISO/IEC 14882:2024 (C++23), was published in October 2024, and C++29 is the next planned version.

Centrally governed city of [[Vietnam]] in the Mekong Delta region (pop., 2024: 4,199,824). It is noted for its floating markets, a village that makes *bánh tráng*, and rural [[Canal|canals]]. Its rivers and canals include the Cần Thơ River, the Hậu River and the Ô Môn Canals. Attractions include the Cái Răng Floating Market and Ninh Kiều Wharf. On June 12, 2025, the National Assembly merged Hậu Giang and Sóc Trăng provinces into the city. Its former central district, Ninh Kiều, is the most populous of the former districts. Academic institutions include Cần Thơ University and Cần Thơ University of Medicine and Pharmacy.

General-purpose programming language created by [[Dennis Ritchie]] at [[Bell Labs]] between 1972 and 1973 as a successor to the B language. It was initially developed to write utilities for Unix and was later used to reimplement the [[Kernel (operating system)|kernel]] of the Unix operating system. C gives programmers relatively direct access to CPU features and is used on machines from [[Supercomputer|supercomputers]] to microcontrollers. It is widely used to implement operating systems, device drivers and protocol stacks, though its use in application software is declining. Standardized by ANSI since 1989 and later jointly by ISO and IEC, it has typically ranked as the most or second-most popular language in the TIOBE index since 2000. *The C Programming Language*, co-authored by Ritchie, served for many years as the de facto standard.

City in central [[Argentina]], capital of Córdoba Province (pop., 2020: about 1.6 million). It is the second-most populous city in the country after [[Buenos Aires]]. Founded on July 6, 1573, by the Spanish conquistador Jerónimo Luis de Cabrera, it was named after the Spanish city of Córdoba. The [[Jesuits]] arrived in 1599 and established the Colegio Máximo, which became the University of Córdoba in 1613 and is now the National University of Córdoba, the oldest university in the country. The Jesuit Block (*Manzana Jesuítica*), a group of 17th-century buildings, was declared a UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]] in 2000. Historical movements include the Cordobazo of May 1969 and the University Revolution of 1918.

American stage musical with music by John Kander, lyrics by Fred Ebb and a book by Joe Masteroff, based on the play *I Am a Camera* (1951), which drew on Christopher Isherwood's 1939 novel *Goodbye to Berlin*. Set in [[Berlin]] in 1929–1930 during the twilight of the [[Weimar Republic]] as the [[Nazi Party|Nazis]] rise to power, it centers on the Kit Kat Klub and the English cabaret performer Sally Bowles. The original Broadway production opened on November 20, 1966, ran for 1,166 performances and won eight Tony Awards. A 1972 film adaptation followed.

Leafy green, red or white biennial plant of the [[Brassicaceae]] family, grown as an annual vegetable for its dense heads. Cabbages comprise several cultivars of *Brassica oleracea* and are closely related to [[Broccoli|broccoli]] and [[Cauliflower|cauliflower]]. A cabbage generally weighs between 500 and 1,000 grams. It was probably domesticated in Europe before 1000 BC and was described as a table luxury in the [[Roman Empire]]. Cabbage became a staple food in central, northern and eastern Europe in the 17th and 18th centuries, and European sailors used it to prevent [[Scurvy|scurvy]]. It is pickled, fermented as in sauerkraut and [[Kimchi|kimchi]], steamed, stewed or eaten raw. [[China]] produces 48% of the world total.

Craft of making cabinets, box-shaped furniture with shelves, drawers or doors for storing or displaying items. Cabinets are typically made of wood, coated steel or synthetic materials, and commercial grades often have a melamine-particleboard core covered in high-pressure laminate. Before [[Industrial design|industrial design]] and the [[Industrial Revolution]], cabinetmakers designed and produced nearly all furniture. The most famous was André-Charles Boulle, whose legacy is known as Boulle work. Mass production gradually took over much of the trade, while the [[Arts and Crafts movement]], begun in the United Kingdom in the mid-19th century, revived handmade work. After [[World War II]], woodworking became a popular [[Hobby|hobby]] among the [[Middle class|middle classes]].

Television programming delivered to viewers by radio-frequency signals carried through coaxial or [[Optical fiber|fiber-optic]] cable. It is distinct from over-the-air terrestrial television and from [[Satellite television]]. In the U.S., the Community Antenna Television (CATV) program of 1948 used large antennas on hills and mountains to serve communities whose terrain blocked broadcast signals. The share of U.S. households with cable rose from 6.4 percent in 1968 to 62.4 percent in 1994. Systems were later upgraded to digital, and most channels are now encrypted, so each television needs its own set-top box. A service drop brings the coaxial cable into the building, and a splitter divides it among rooms. Cable lines also carry FM radio and high-speed Internet service.

Class of [[Transport|transport]] modes that use cables to carry passengers and goods, often in vehicles called cable cars. The cable may be driven or passive, and loads move by pulling, sliding or sailing on cableways, with [[Pulley|pulleys]] and balanced loads as common elements. Such systems are often used in mountainous areas to overcome large differences in elevation. Major types include aerial transport, in which cars hang from cables strung between supports, and cable railways, in which cars on steep rails are hauled by cable, such as funiculars. The first funicular railway opened in Lyon in 1862. In [[San Francisco]], Andrew Hallidie opened the Clay Street Hill Railroad on August 2, 1873, the first effective and commercially successful cable-car route.

[[Algorithm|Algorithms]] that decide which data a computer cache discards when it is full and new data must be stored. Caching keeps recent or often-used data in memory that is faster to access than main memory. Replacement strategies trade hit rate against latency: more efficient ones track more usage information, while faster ones track less. Bélády's algorithm, the optimal policy, discards the item needed furthest in the future, but this cannot be predicted in practice. Common policies include first-in, first-out (FIFO), least recently used (LRU) and least frequently used (LFU).

Plant of the family Cactaceae, mostly succulent and adapted to dry environments. The family comprises 131–140 genera and some 1,866 up to 2000+ known species, native to the [[Americas]] from Patagonia to western Canada, with one species also found in Africa and Sri Lanka. Cacti store water in thickened stems, which also carry out [[Photosynthesis|photosynthesis]]. Most species have lost true [[Leaf|leaves]], keeping spines, which are modified leaves that reduce water loss and deter [[Herbivore|herbivores]]. Spines and flowers arise from areoles, an identifying feature of cacti. Many have ribs in Fibonacci numbers that let stems expand after rain. Their [[Transpiration|transpiration]] occurs at night, reducing water loss. The tallest free-standing cactus, *Pachycereus pringlei*, reaches 19.2 m (63 ft).

British multinational confectionery company, headquartered in [[Buckinghamshire]]. Founded in [[Birmingham]], England, in 1824 by the Quaker John Cadbury, who sold [[Tea|tea]], [[Coffee|coffee]] and drinking [[Chocolate|chocolate]]. Its Dairy Milk chocolate, introduced in 1905, was the company's best-selling product by 1914. Owned by [[Mondelez International]] since 2010, the company operates in more than 50 countries and is the second-largest confectionery brand in the world after Mars.

[[Chemical element]] with symbol Cd and atomic number 48, a soft, silvery-white metal. It resembles [[Zinc|zinc]] and [[Mercury (element)|mercury]], the other stable group 12 metals, and usually has oxidation state +2. Its average concentration in Earth's crust is between 0.1 and 0.5 parts per million. Cadmium was discovered in 1817 in Germany as an impurity in zinc carbonate, and it occurs in most zinc ores as a byproduct of zinc production. It was long used as corrosion-resistant plating on [[Steel|steel]] and in red, orange and yellow pigments. Because cadmium is toxic, its use is declining, and nickel–cadmium batteries have largely been replaced by nickel–metal hydride and lithium-ion types. As a neutron poison, it is used in control rods of nuclear reactors, and cadmium telluride is used in some solar panels.

Order of limbless, worm-like or snake-like [[Amphibian|amphibians]], Gymnophiona, with small eyes or none. Caecilians mostly live hidden in soil or streambeds in the tropics of South and Central America, Africa and southern Asia, feeding on small subterranean animals such as [[Earthworm|earthworms]]. Their skulls are bullet-shaped and strongly built, and their slimy skin has ring-like grooves; some species have scales beneath it. The name Gymnophiona derives from Greek words meaning naked and snake, because caecilians were once thought to be related to snakes. More than 220 living species are classified in 10 families. Caecilians are one of three living amphibian groups, alongside [[Frog|frogs]] and [[Salamander|salamanders]].

Free-living, transparent [[Nematode|nematode]] about 1 mm long, the type species of its genus. It lives in temperate soils and has a mouth, pharynx, intestine and gonad, but no circulatory or respiratory system. Most individuals are hermaphrodites, and about one in a thousand is male. Sydney Brenner proposed research on *C. elegans* in 1963, and it became a widely used [[Model organism|model organism]] in molecular and developmental biology. It was the first multicellular organism to have its whole genome sequenced, and in 2019 it was the first with its connectome, the complete map of its wiring. It has 302 [[Neuron|neurons]]. Work on it has won four Nobel Prizes as of 2024.

One of the simplest and most widely known [[Encryption|encryption]] techniques in [[Cryptography|cryptography]], in which each letter is replaced by a letter a fixed number of positions along the alphabet. With a shift of three, A becomes D. The method is named after [[Julius Caesar]], who used it in his private correspondence. Shifts wrap around from Z to A, and the shift serves as the key. As a single-alphabet substitution, it is easily broken and offers essentially no communications security. Its ROT13 variant, a shift of 13, remains in use for mild obfuscation.

Green [[Salad|salad]] of romaine lettuce and croutons, commonly dressed with [[Lemon|lemon]] juice, olive oil, eggs, Worcestershire sauce, anchovies, garlic, Parmesan and black pepper. The Italian immigrant restaurateur Caesar Cardini created it on July 4, 1924, at his restaurant Caesar's in [[Tijuana]], Mexico, when a holiday rush left the kitchen short of ingredients. It was prepared tableside and is still prepared that way at the original restaurant. A popular myth credits [[Julius Caesar]], but the salad is generally attributed to Cardini. [[Julia Child]] said she ate one at Cardini's in the 1920s, made with whole romaine leaves.

Surgical delivery of one or more babies through an incision in the mother's abdomen, also called C-section. It is often performed when vaginal delivery would risk injury or death, for reasons including obstructed labor, twin pregnancy, breech birth and placental problems. The [[Surgery|operation]] typically takes 45 minutes to an hour, under a spinal block or [[Anesthesia|general anesthesia]]. The [[World Health Organization|WHO]] recommends it only when medically necessary. About 23 million were performed globally in 2012. The claim that [[Julius Caesar]] was born this way is probably a misconception, since his mother survived his birth.

Radioactive isotope of caesium that forms as one of the more common [[Nuclear fission|fission]] products of [[Uranium-235|uranium-235]] in nuclear reactors and weapons. Its [[Half-life|half-life]] is about 30.04 years, and it decays by beta emission to stable barium-137. Its gamma rays, at 0.6617 MeV, come from the metastable barium-137m. Because its compounds are water-soluble salts and the element becomes volatile at high temperature, it spreads widely after release, as in the Chernobyl accident. Caesium-137 is used to calibrate radiation detectors, in [[Radiation therapy|radiation therapy]], and in industrial gauges and flow meters.

[[Chemical element]] with symbol Cs and atomic number 55, a soft, silvery-golden [[Alkali metal|alkali metal]] with a melting point of 28.5 °C. It is one of only five elemental metals that are liquid at or near room temperature, and it is pyrophoric, reacting with water even at −116 °C. Discovered in 1860 by Robert Bunsen and [[Gustav Kirchhoff]] through [[Spectroscopy|flame spectroscopy]], it was first used as a getter in vacuum tubes and in photoelectric cells. Since 1967 the second has been defined by a hyperfine transition of caesium-133 atoms, and caesium is widely used in highly accurate [[Atomic clock|atomic clocks]]. Its largest modern application is as caesium formate in drilling fluids. The radioactive isotope [[Caesium-137]] is used in medical applications, industrial gauges and hydrology. The name comes from the Latin *caesius*, meaning bluish grey.

Central nervous system [[Stimulant|stimulant]] of the methylxanthine class, and the most commonly consumed psychoactive drug globally. It is a bitter, white crystalline purine [[Alkaloid|alkaloid]] related to the adenine and guanine bases of DNA and RNA. It occurs in the seeds, leaves and fruits of plants native to [[Africa]], [[East Asia]] and South America, where it deters herbivores. Its main human sources are the leaves of [[Camellia sinensis]] ([[Tea|tea]]) and [[Coffee|coffee]] beans, and it works largely by blocking adenosine receptors. Some people experience sleep disruption or anxiety from caffeine, and regular use can produce mild dependence, with withdrawal symptoms such as sleepiness, headache and irritability. The European Food Safety Authority considers up to 400 mg a day unlikely to raise safety concerns for non-pregnant adults.
